Deeper insights into the drug defense of glioma cells against
hydrophobic molecules
Valeria Verebovaa, Dominik Belejb, Jaroslava Joniovab, Zuzana Jurasekovab,c,
Pavol Miskovskyb,c, Tibor Kozarc, Denis Horvathc, Jana Stanicovaa,d,
Veronika Huntosovac,*
a Institute of Biophysics, University of Veterinary Medicine and Pharmacy, Komenskeho 73, 041 81 Kosice, Slovakia
b Department of Biophysics, Faculty of Science, P. J. Safarik University in Kosice, Jesenna 5, 041 54 Kosice, Slovakia

Keywords:
Glioma cells
Selective photo-activation
Hypericin
Antraquinones
P-glycoprotein
A B S T R A C T
By means of ﬂuorescence microscopy the intracellular distribution of ﬂuorescent drugs with different
hydrophobicity (quinizarin, emodin and hypericin) was studied. Selective photoactivation of these drugs
in precisely deﬁned position (nuclear envelope) allowed moderately hydrophobic emodin enter the
nucleus. Highly hydrophobic hypericin was predominantly kept in the membranes with no ﬂuorescence
observed in the nucleus. The redistribution of quinizarin, emodin and hypericin between lipids, proteins
and DNA was studied in solutions and cells. Based on these results was proposed theoretical model of
hydrophobic drugs’ nuclear internalization after photo-activation. Molecular docking models showed
that hypericin has the strongest afﬁnity to P-glycoprotein involved in the cell detoxiﬁcation. Presence of
10 mM quinizarin, emodin or hypericin increased P-glycoprotein function in U87 MG cells. Moreover,
emodin pretreatment allowed quinizarin nuclear internalization without photo-activation, which was
not the case for hypericin. The synergy of such pretreatment and photo-activation should lessen the drug
doses with simultaneous increase of drug efﬁcacy triggering cell apoptosis/necrosis.

1. Introduction
The hydrophobicity of anticancer drugs and concept of their
transport into targeted tissue is of interest for numerous cancer
treatments. For the efﬁcient transport drugs must be hydrophobic
enough to enter the lipid bilayer, but they should also be able to be
released from the membranes (Kubinyi, 1979). Hence, drug
hydrophobicity plays a key role in its distribution, metabolism
and clearance from the body (Eisenberg and McLachlan, 1986;
Miyamoto and Kollman, 1993). Hypericin, quinizarin and emodin
are naturally occurring plant pigments that possess anti-viral, anti-
tumoral and anti-inﬂammatory properties (Andersen et al., 1991;
Ma et al., 2003; Mueller et al., 1998; Nemeikaite-Ceniene et al.,
2002; Quinti et al., 2003). These planar, aromatic organic
compounds are redox catalysts and play an important role in
many processes, e.g. electron transport, photosynthesis or cellular
respiration (Bogdanska et al., 1999). Their inﬂuence on cell death
pathways has been widely studied either in dark condition or after
light-activation (Andersen et al., 1991; Huntosova et al., 2012;
Mikesova et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 1998; Rossi et al., 2010). Also
their molecular interactions with DNA were already studied
(Miskovsky et al., 1995b; Saito et al., 2012; Verebova et al., 2014), to
our knowledge no direct evidence of nuclear localization has been
reported yet. The nuclear envelope (NcE) is considered to be the
main barrier that protects nuclear DNA from interaction with
anticancer drugs. Another problem for cancer treatment effective-
ness is multi-drug resistance accompanied by decrease of drug
accumulation in the resistant cells, due to active efﬂux of these
drugs mainly by P-glycoprotein (P-gp) (Gottesman et al., 2002;
Gottesman and Pastan, 1993). Photochemical activation at speciﬁc
point/organelle within cells (Weyergang et al., 2015) is one of the
possibilities how to overpass drug-resistance of the cancer cells.
The second choice could be moderate regulation of P-gp activity as
it was demonstrated in a wide variety of human cancer cells,

including glioblastoma (U87 MG) (Kondo et al., 1996; Regina et al.,
2001; Rittierodt et al., 2004). The role of P-gp is to detoxify cells by
exporting chemically unrelated toxins (Aller et al., 2009). In this
context and based on our previous works (Miskovsky et al., 1995a,
1995b; SanchezCortes et al., 1996), we evaluated using various
experimental and theoretical approaches to both analyze distri-
bution pattern for selected organic compounds as well as set up
methodologies with aim to increase the drugs intracellular uptake
and nuclear targeting. We have demonstrated that increase of the
intracellular concentration of the small hydrophobic molecules
takes place either by regulation of P-gp activity or by selective
light-activation of these photosensitive molecules. This would
importantly inﬂuence the targeting and induction of cell death
pathways, apoptosis/necrosis.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Chemicals
Hypericin (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) was dissolved in dimethyl
sulfoxide (DMSO, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) to a ﬁnal concentration of
2 mM. Emodin (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) and quinizarin (Sigma-
Aldrich, Germany) were dissolved in DMSO to the ﬁnal concentra-
tion of 10 mM. Albumin from human serum (HSA, Sigma-Aldrich,
USA) and low-density lipoproteins extracted from human serum
(LDL, Invitrogen, Life science, France) were dissolved in 0.9%
isotonic aqueous solution of NaCl (0.9% NaCl, Braun, Germany) to
the concentration of 10 nM. Deoxyribonucleic acid sodium salt
from calf thymus (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) was dissolved at
concentration of 2.3 mM in TRIS (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) buffer at pH
7.4. Anti-P Glycoprotein antibody (ab129450, Abcam, United
Kingdom) and anti-PKCa pThr638 antibody (E195ab, Novus
Europe) were used as primary antibodies for immunohistochem-
istry. Alexa Fluor1488 (LifeTechnologies, France) was used as
secondary antibody. A nuclear probe Hoechst 33342 (Hoechst,
Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) was dissolved in aqueous solution to
1.6 mM 
concentration. 
Solution 
of 
100% 
methanol 
(Merck,
Germany) was used for cell ﬁxation. For all measurement the
ﬁnal content of DMSO was less than 1%.
2.2. Cell culture
U87 MG human glioma cells (Cells Lines Services, Germany)
were plated and maintained according to propagation protocols
onto 35 mm culture dishes with integral No. 0 glass cover slip
bottoms (MatTek, USA). The U87 MG cells were grown in
Dulbecco’s modiﬁed Eagle medium (D-MEM), containing L-
glutamine 
(862 mg/L), 
sodium 
pyruvate 
(110 mg/L), 
glucose
(4500 mg/L), streptomycin (50 mg/mL) and supplemented with
10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), in the presence of 5% CO2 hummiﬁed
atmosphere at 37 C. All chemicals were purchased from Gibco-
Invitrogen, Life Technologies Ltd. Cells were incubated in the dark.
After reaching 40–50% conﬂuence, cells were used in experiments
according protocols described below.
2.3. Intracellular distribution of drugs
The U87 MG cells were treated with 10 mM hypericin, emodin
or quinizarin for 24 h. The concentration 10 mM was chosen with
the aim to increase the ﬂuorescence intensity and resolution of the
micro-images. This concentration of the studied molecules is able
to oversaturate the 
organelles 
in 
such 
manner, 
that 
their
ﬂuorescence is partially quenched by an aggregation process
within these organelles (the process is explained in Huntosova
et al., 2010), the free molecules in the cytoplasm can pass into the
nucleus and it does not induce rapid cellular death. The 24 h
incubation time was in accordance with literature (Huntosova
et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014). Such timing should enhance (maximize)
the ability of the drugs to enter the nucleus with simultaneous
prevention of the cells from rapid death.
In order to assess intracellular localization pattern in U87 MG
cells, experiments were performed under two different conditions.
In the ﬁrst case, exponentially growing cells were treated in the
presence of drug (10 mM aqueous solution of hypericin, emodin or
quinizarin) for 24 h prior to detection. Alternatively, cells were ﬁrst
ﬁxed in ice cold 100% methanol for 1hr at 20 C and then
incubated with drug (10 mM hypericin, emodin or quinizarin in
distilled water) for 24 h at room temperature and in dark.
After incubation the cells were washed and assessed with a 63X
oil 
objective 
(NA 
1.46) 
of 
LSM 
700 
confocal 
ﬂuorescence
microscope system (LSM, Zeiss, Germany). Excitation of hypericin
was performed with 555 nm solid laser and quinizarin was excited
with 488 nm solid laser. The detection window was chosen 580–
630 nm for hypericin and 500–630 nm for quinizarin and emodin.
The power of the lasers was not higher than 10% of the total power.
Fluorescence signals were analyzed by the ZEN 2011 software
(Zeiss, Germany). The plot proﬁles from the region of interests
were measured in Image J software (National Institutes of Health,
Bethesda, Maryland).
The nuclear localization was validated with staining of native
and ﬁxed cells with a nuclear probe Hoechst at the excitation
405 nm and the ﬂuorescence was collected in the spectral range
420–500 nm.
2.4. Theoretical modeling of intracellular distribution and dynamics of
drugs
The dynamics of intracellular distribution for hydrophobic
drugs and their transport within the cells were analyzed using a
top-down qualitative compartmental model (Patra and Klumpp,
2014). The model was proposed as a set of qualitative differential
equations. The structure and parametric choices are still in a
conceptual stage but they seek to integrate our qualitative
knowledge about the observed system. Four compartments have
been considered and denoted as F (free drug compartment), O
(organelle compartment), NcE (nuclear envelope compartment)
and N (nuclear compartment). The concentrations of the drug
inside these compartments are denoted CX with the transition rates
kXY, where X and Y can be substituted by F, O, NcE or N.
Redistribution of drugs between the compartments can be
described with the phenomenological equations with the assump-
tion that the levels of CO,CNcE and CN are mediated by CF. There was
given assumption that concentration CF plays a role of the common
factor what means it has access to each compartment. Further-
more, the reversible kinetics can be expressed in four equations by
general build up principles (Upadhay, 2006; Vriens, 1954) as
follows:
dCF/dt = JF + kOFCO + kNcEFCNcE + kNFCN  CF(kFO + kFNcE + kFN) 
(1)
dCO/dt = kFOCF  kOFCO, 
(2)
dCNcE/dt = kFNcECF  kNcEFCNcE, 
(3)
dCN/dt = kFNCN  kNFCN. 
(4)
A balance between drug injection ﬂow (administration of the
drug into the system) JF
(of 
the extracellular origin) and
intracellular 
transfer 
dCF/dt + dCO/dt + dCNcE/dt + dCN/dt 
can 
be

veriﬁed by substituting of the derivatives from the previous
equations into:
JF = dCF/dt + dCO/dt + dCNcE/dt + dCN/dt. 
(5)
The 
drug 
redistribution 
between 
the 
compartments 
is
characterized by the system of kXY reaction rates. The injection
of “free” drug can be modeled by the ﬂow injection described in
the form:
JF(t) = JFO if tFD < t < tFU, otherwise JF(t) = 0 
(6)
where the occurrence of nonzero and positive amplitude JF(t) = JFO
is bounded to the injection time interval [tFD, tFU].
If the drug concentration exceeds critical value and the laser
radiation is applied (t = tPH, tPH > tFU), then the kinetic constant
changes and it will inﬂuence kNF and kFN in such a manner that the
drug transfer between compartments F and N can be expressed in
relations:
kNF(t) = predeﬁned constant 6¼ 0 if t > tPH and CNcE(t)  CNcETH,
otherwise kNF(t) = kNF(t  0+), 
(7)
where kFN(t  0+), kNF(t  0+) denote the “previous” kFN(t) and kNF(t)
values respectively, which is speciﬁc for the integrator and
integration step (TH means threshold value). In the case of non-
damaged NcE the initial conditions are
kFN(t = 0) = 0 and kFN(t = 0) = 0. 
(8)
CNcETH is the constant threshold level of CNcE(t) sufﬁcient for the
NcE penetration. The logical and operator implies that the
simultaneous presence of laser radiation and super threshold
concentration is required. The complex deﬁnitions of kFN(t) and
kNF(t) make the whole system of equations substantially nonlinear.
In our calculation it is assumed that highly hydrophobic
molecules can have high afﬁnity to the organelles and weak afﬁnity
to the nucleus, therefore
kOF < kNcEF < kNF, kFO > kFNcE > kFN. 
(9)
In order to simplify the system new positively independent
parameters were introduced ka, kb and dk with the following
relationship: ka > kb > 6 dk. The auxiliary parametrization allows
deﬁnition of transparently two distinct systems:
i) hydrophobic drugs with stronger afﬁnity to the nucleus
(intercalators) characterized by following parameters: kFO = ka,
kOF = kb, kFNcE = ka  dk, kNcEF = kb + dk, kFN = ka  2dk, kNF = kb + 2dk.
ii) hydrophobic drugs with low afﬁnity to the nucleus which differ
in kFN and kNF values accordingly: kFN = ka  3dk and kNF = kb +
3dk.
It should be noted, that only arbitrary units and qualitative
comparison have been monitored to check the quality and
importance of the preliminary results. For the numerical simu-
lations the parameters were chosen as follows: ka = 0.5, kb = 0.1,
dk = 0.03, tFD = 0.01, tFU = 0.02, tPH = 0.1 and CNcETH = 0.01. Let us
emphasize that the purpose of the parametric settings is not
intended to present absolute predictions but rather to gain insights
into the behavior of the compartments.
2.5. Selective photo-activation of drugs
The U87 MG cells were treated for 24 h with 10 mM hypericin or
emodin in dark. After treatment, cells were washed and the
ﬂuorescence images were collected with using 63X oil objective of
the confocal ﬂuorescence microscope system. Laser light at 405 nm
was used for excitation of both molecules. Hypericin and emodin
emission was collected in the spectral range of 500–630 nm.
Irradiation of nuclear envelope (NcE) was performed with the
same laser, but the power was increased up to 40% of total laser
power. Irradiation time was not longer than 1 min (one scan time).
The ﬂuorescence image was detected right after irradiation and
5 min after irradiation. Fluorescence signals were analyzed using
the ZEN 2011 software. The plot proﬁles from the area of interest
were obtained with using Image J software and plotted in
OriginLab1 software.
2.6. Redistribution of drugs into LDL or HSA in solution
The complexes of DNA-drug, LDL-drug and HSA-drug were
prepared one day before the experiments to reach the equilibrium.
For that, aliquot amounts of 10 nM aqueous solutions of DNA, LDL
or HSA and of 10 mM stock solutions of hypericin, emodin or
quinizarin were used. The ﬂuorescence spectra of these complexes
were measured in 3 ml quartz cuvette using a spectroﬂuorometer
(RF-5301 PC, SHIMADZU, Japan) at excitation 555, 405 or 488 nm
and the emission was collected from 420–750 or 550–750 nm.
Firstly, the redistribution of hypericin, emodin or quinizarin
from DNA-drug complexes towards LDL or HSA was observed in
such a way that 3 ml of 10 mM LDL solution or 3 ml of 10 mM HSA
solution were added 3 times to the solution of the complex. The
ﬂuorescence spectra were recorded immediately (5 s) after every
addition. Similar LDL- and HSA-drug complexes were initially
prepared and then 150 ml of DNA (100 mM) was added in order to
observe possible redistribution of the molecules from LDL or HSA
towards DNA. The ﬂuorescence spectra were registered before and
after addition of the DNA solution.
2.7. Fluorescence spectroscopy
Denatured DNA was prepared by heating of the 2.3 mM DNA
solution up to 90 C for 1 h. After 1 h the solution was cooled down
to room temperature. The complexes of native and denatured DNA
with hypericin, emodin and quinizarin (1:105 bp) were prepared
24 h prior to measurement. The spectra were collected as
mentioned above.
All the measurements were performed at least twice.
2.8. Fluorescence lifetime imaging
Fixed cells, treated with 10 mM hypericin according to the
protocol mentioned above, were detected with ﬂuorescence
lifetime imaging system (FLIM, DSC-120 Dual Channel Confocal
Scanning system, Becker & Hickl GmbH, Germany) using inverted
ﬂuorescence 
microscope 
(Zeiss 
AxioObserver 
Z1, 
Germany)
equipped with 40X water immersion objective (Zeiss, Germany).
Hypericin was excited with 470 nm light (5% power) from NKT-
Super-K Extreme laser (NKT Photonics, Denmark) and its ﬂuores-
cence lifetimes were detected with HPM-100-40 hybrid detector
(Becker & Hickl GmbH, Germany) ﬁltered with LP 485 and BP
624  20 nm in the 25 ns time range. The time decays were
analyzed with SPC image analysis software (Becker &Hickl GmbH,
Germany).
2.9. Localization of P-gp and PKCa in U87 MG cells
U87 MG cells were treated with 10 mM hypericin, emodin or
quinizarin for 30 min in dark. After incubation the cells were
washed and ﬁxed with 100% methanol for 1 h at 20 C. After
ﬁxation, cells were washed three times with 0.2% BSA/PBS.
Subsequently, cells were incubated with blocking buffer for 1 h
in PBS containing 1% BSA, 10% goat serum, 0.4 mM Mg2+ and

0.2 mM Ca2+ at 37 C to block unspeciﬁc labelling. After three
washes with 0.2% BSA/PBS, cells were incubated with speciﬁc
primary antibodies (Ab) against P-gp or phosphorylated PKCa at
threonine 638 (pPKCa(Thr638)) for 1 h at 37 C. Then cells were
washed three times with 0.2% BSA/PBS followed by 1 h incubation
with secondary Ab AlexaFluor1488 at 37 C. The after, cells were
washed three times with 0.2% BSA/PBS to remove unbound
secondary Ab and placed into 0.2% BSA/PBS until processing.
Samples were measured by confocal ﬂuorescence microscope
(mentioned above), with 488 nm solid laser excitation and 500–
580 nm detection window. The power of the laser was not higher
than 4% of total power. Fluorescence signals were analyzed by the
Zen 2011 software (Zeiss, Germany).
2.10. Emodin pre-treatment
The U87 MG cells were treated with 10 mM emodin for 30 min.
Then, the culture medium was removed and replaced with
medium containing either 10 mM hypericin or quinizarin for
24 h (until imaging). Fluorescence images were collected with
confocal-ﬂuorescence 
microscope 
and 
analyzed 
with 
Zen
2011 software as mentioned above.
2.11. Molecular docking
Two different program suites and docking protocols were used
at ﬁrst in order to assess the P-gp binding of the substances under
study: the CDOCKER (Wu et al., 2003) protocol of Discovery Studio
Modeling Environment of Biovia (2015) and GLIDE from the
Schrödinger Suite of Programs (2015). The crystal structure 3G60
(Aller et al., 2009) of mouse P-gp that has 87% overall sequence
identity with human ortholog was acquired from PDB (Berman
et al., 2000). The downloaded structure was processed using the
“Protein Preparation” wizard of Maestro from the Schrödinger
Suite of Programs (2015). The ligand geometries were optimized at
ﬁrst with Jaguar (DFT B3LYP/6-31G**) (Bochevarov et al., 2013). The
structures thus obtained were docked into the protein binding site
using both, CDOCKER (Wu et al., 2003) and GLIDE (Friesner et al.,
2004; Halgren et al., 2004) and then redocked using the Quantum
Polarized Ligand Docking (QPLD) protocol (Cho et al., 2005), the

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Nuclear targeting via selective photo-activation of drugs in
nuclear envelope of U87 MG cells
Emodin (AlogP = 2.568), hypericin (AlogP = 5.040) and quini-
zarin (AlogP = 2.324) were chosen as the representatives (and
model systems) of moderately hydrophobic, highly hydrophobic
and intercalator molecules that can be favorably used in cancer
therapy. Fig. 1 illustrates the intracellular distribution of these
molecules in U87 MG glioma cells. Cell ﬁxation allowed passive
diffusion of drugs in the cells. Taking into account that the
intracellular concentration is related to the recorded ﬂuorescence
intensity it can be seen that cell distribution and drug accumula-
tion after 24 h treatment is very similar among all used drug
molecules. In addition, the most intense areas are localized in the
perinuclear region where mitochondria, lysosomes, endoplasmic
reticulum and Golgi apparatus are present (Huntosova et al., 2012)
(Fig. 1). If we consider that Hoechst staining (Fig. 1D) possesses
maximum ﬂuorescence intensity in the chromatin part, than only
6% of this intensity can be found in the nucleolus and no intensity
out of the nucleus. In further approximation, similarly for cells
incubated with hypericin, emodin or quinizarine the maximum of
ﬂuorescence intensity can be identiﬁed. However, for these cells
the maximum ﬂuorescence intensity is out of the nucleus in the
perinuclear area. The ﬂuorescence of chromatin area decreases to
33% for hypericin and quinizarin, and only 6% for emodin. The
nucleolus ﬂuorescence increases to 100% for hypericin and emodin,
66% for quinizarin. Interestingly, under studied experimental
conditions none of these molecules penetrated into the intact
nucleus although they strongly ﬂuoresced in the NcE (data not
shown). This suggests that the cell’s protective system conserves
the molecules to stay localized outside from the nucleus. In
consequence, ﬂuorescence spectra of hypericin, emodin and
quinizarin were detected in the presence of native and denatured
DNA with the aim to distinguish whether the increase of the intra-
nuclear ﬂuorescence comes from enlarged number of molecules or
from phenomenon of DNA denaturation (Fig. 1E–G). The most
prominent changes were observed in the case of quinizarin where
the molecule’s ﬂuorescence increases signiﬁcantly in the presence
of denatured DNA. It can be assumed that DNA denaturation
enlarged the distances between individual quinizarin molecules
(ﬂuorescence quenching decreases) and helps to visualize the
molecules inside the DNA.
In order to understand intranuclear ﬂuorescence intensity
decrease, ﬂuorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) was performed.
Due to spectroscopic properties and lifetimes detection abilities
further for FLIM experiment only the most hydrophobic hypericin
was chosen. The intensities of the molecules ﬂuorescence can be
particularly affected by saturation of bio-molecules and by Förster
energy transfer between molecules or selfquenching (Huntosova
et al., 2010). The results of ﬂuorescence lifetime’s distribution
obtained for hypericin within the ﬁxed cells are shown in Fig. 2.
Higher afﬁnity of hypericin towards lipids results in intense
ﬂuorescence attributed mainly to its monomeric form (Gbur et al.,
2008; Huntosova et al., 2010), also characterized by the ﬂuores-
cence lifetimes tL  6 ns (Fig. 2B) (Taroni et al., 2005). On the other
site, proteins presence will mostly quench it due to the fast
proteins oversaturation by hypericin (Hritz et al., 2002). This
ﬂuorescence quenching can be recognized on hypericin ﬂuores-
cence lifetimes in the nucleolus. The lifetimes decrease from
6 ns < tL down to 3 ns < tL < 6 ns (Fig. 2B). The most signiﬁcant
ﬂuorescence lifetime decrease was observed for hypericin local-
ized in the nucleus, at the place of chromatin occurrence (Fig. 2B,
C). Measured lifetimes had values tL < 3 ns, which implies
aggregation process as it was observed in the presence of LDL or
cells (Gbur et al., 2008; Huntosova et al., 2010; Taroni et al., 2005).
In further, selective photo-activation was used to enable drugs
passive diffusion into nucleus.
The results of selective photo-activation of hypericin and
emodin in glioma cells are summarized in Fig. 3. The photo-
damage induced in NcE can be observed by a speciﬁcally localized
decrease in ﬂuorescence intensity as compared with the non-
irradiated cells. Five minutes after the photo-treatment, emodin

3.3. Theoretical modeling of drug redistribution and nuclear targeting
A qualitative model for hydrophobic drugs (possessing similar
properties as hypericin, emodin and quinizarin) intra-cellular
transport was proposed (see Section 2.4). Two distinct systems
were deﬁned. Less hydrophobic drugs as emodin or quinizarin can
pass the plasma membrane and in further they are trapped by
organelles and proteins or other biomacromolecules nearby. After
light stimulus, they can easily pass the NcE and remain inside
nucleus, where they can interact with DNA or other messengers of
cell death. On the other hand, highly hydrophobic molecules with
lipophilic character, like hypericin, can pass the plasma membrane,
but due to their lipophilicity they can remain in the organelles in
cytoplasm. Lipophilic character of these molecules can enlarge the
time of their penetration into the nucleus and its high hydropho-
bicity can cause even their aggregation accompanied with
ﬂuorescence quenching (Huntosova et al., 2010).
The simulation results of the qualitative compartmental
approach are depicted in Fig. 5. The graphs show time dependence
(time t is rescaled by tPH) of the concentrations in the compart-
ments F (free drug compartment), O (organelle compartment), NcE
(nuclear envelope compartment) and N (nuclear compartment).
The system of concentrations is allowed to evolve from the initial
condition

3.4. P-glycoprotein—emodin, hypericin and quinizarin interaction
proﬁles
As it was shown above intrancellular and intranuclear drug
concentration can be increased with photo-activation. Another
possibility can be regulation of P-gp function, as it was observed in
the cancer cells treated with doxorubicin (Szaﬂarski et al., 2013).
Fig. 6A represents the P-gp distribution in non-treated control
U87 MG glioma cells. The majority of P-gp is localized in cytoplasm
whereas only small part can be observed in the nucleus. In
addition, there is no signiﬁcant presence of P-gp in the NcE. In the
treated glioma cells the amount of P-gp in cytoplasm dramatically
increased and singular spots of P-gp in NcE can be clearly observed
(Fig. 6C, F, I). Moreover, in the case of emodin treatment, even
higher localization of P-gp within the nucleus can be identiﬁed
(Fig. 6C). It can be assumed that P-gp present in the nucleus
protects cells against drug toxicity and importantly affects drug’s
efﬂux from the cells.
Considering the observed intracellular localization of P-pg the
interest was given to the estimation anthraquinone derivatives
binding afﬁnities towards P-gp. The P-gp comprises four domains
in a single polypeptide chain. Two transmembrane domains form
the ligand binding site and two nucleotide-binding domains bind
and hydrolyze ATP to proceed to the substrate translocation
(Becker et al., 2009). The detailed interaction proﬁle of emodin
with P-gp based on the CDOCKER results has already been

3.5. Drugs nuclear targeting by regulation of P-glycoprotein function
In the previous studies emodin has been identiﬁed as an
important agent, which can strongly regulate P-gp function in vitro
(Li et al., 2014). In experimental protocols adapted from available
literature effect of combination treatment with emodin followed
by hypericin or quinizarin treatment on U87 MG cells was tested as
follows: (i) ﬁrstly, cells were pretreated for 30 min with 10 mM
emodin (it can inhibit P-gp activity down to 50% (Li et al., 2014));
and in the next (ii) 24 h treatment with 10 mM hypericin or
quinizarin was applied.
P-gp distribution in U87 MG cells after emodin pretreatment is
showed in Fig. 7B. As it was previously shown (Fig. 6C) P-gp is
mostly localized in perinuclear area and in NcE. The important role
in the cell death and proliferation plays PKCa as a factor which is
involved in the protective response of cells in the apoptotic
pathway (Nakashima, 2002). PKCa was also identiﬁed as one of the
enzymes which can regulate the expression of P-gp by its
phosphorylation (Davies et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2012). Catalytically
competent (active fraction) form of PKCa characterized by
phosphorylation on Threonine 638 is shown in Fig. 7C. Important-
ly, common localization of P-gp and pPKCa(Thr638) can be
identiﬁed in the NcE (Fig. 7B, C). This could suggest direct relation
for PKCa and P-gp in emodin pretreated cells. However, it is known
that this is not the only one PKC isoform, which can phosphorylate
P-gp (Fine et al., 1996; Sachs et al., 1999). Subcellular localization of
emodin in native U87 MG cells is presented in Fig. 7A.
Fluorescence of hypericin and quinizarin in U87 MG without
and with combination treatment are presented in Fig. 8. Emodin
pretreatment leads to morphological changes of glioma cells
further treated with hypericin, which can trigger one of the cell

This pretreatment however increased hypericin intracellular
concentration, but its ﬂuorescence was not observed in the
nucleus. On the contrary, after emodin pretreatment, quinizarin
can be found also inside the nucleus. This suggests that drug with

4. Conclusion
The increasing of intracellular concentration without increasing
of applied drug doses is big challenge for cancer treatments.
Present study demonstrates two approaches how to achieve it.
Nucleus was targeted either by selective photo-activation or by P-
gp function regulation. First approach, selective photo-activation
in NcE, allowed less hydrophobic emodin to enter the nucleus. New
concept how to study distributions of hydrophobic drugs before
and after photo-activation in U87 MG cancer cells by implemen-
tation of experimental and theoretical approaches was presented.
The second approach employed P-gp regulation in U87 MG cells by
hypericin, emodin and quinizarin themselves. P-gp expression was
higher after treatment with all studied molecules and molecular
docking method identiﬁed hypericin as the strongest binder to P-
gp among them. The combination treatment was shown to be
effective. Emodin pre-treatment resulted in quinizarin ability to
pass through the NcE and accumulate in the nucleus. This effect
was not observed for more hydrophobic hypericin, but hypericin
intracellular concentration increased. Such combination could be
even effective when using selective transport systems. Precise
mechanism and the role in the cell death pathways is the object for
further study.
